newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Trading gains boost Kredietbank first-half profit.
newsitem.headline: Trading gains boost Kredietbank first-half profit.

text.p: A sharp rise in trading profit boosted Belgian Kredietbank's first-half 1996 earnings, but the bank smoothed out the rise by booking higher provisions.

The bank said on Thursday its consolidated operating profit rose 47.8 pct to 18.66 billion francs ($599 million) from 12.62 billion, mainly due to income from exchange activities and trading, which soared to 3.68 billion francs from just 0.95 billion in the first half.

But the bank also nearly doubled its provisions to 7.87 billion francs, which limited the increase in bottom-line profit. Its group net profit rose 14.5 percent to 6.69 billion francs from 5.84 billion.
"We follow a careful policy. We do not allow all profit that we make to end up in the bottom line," Kredietbank chief executive officer Marcel Cockaerts told a news conference in reply to a question.
He said he expected a "very good" full-year 1996 profit.
"We are full of confidence that full year results will be very good," he said.

Cockaerts also said that an internal audit carried out following recent allegations of tax evasion at sister bank Kredietbank SA Luxembourgoise had revealed no involvement of tax evasion in its own accounts.
"We have found no indication whatsoever of involvement in fraudulent fiscal constructions," he said.
He added that the bank had not been approached by judicial authorities. "We are not aware that any judicial investigation is under way," he said.
He said the bank had not made any provisions in connection with the Luxembourg allegations. "In the current state of the affair there is no need to make provisions," he said.
The bank also said that its foreign expansion strategy was focused on those areas which have the strongest economic growth.
"Our foreign expansion is not focused strongly on Europe. Europe is overbanked and economic growth there is slow," Cockaerts said.
Kredietbank's approach is in stark contrast with Generale Bank, Belgium's biggest bank, which has focused its foreign operations in a 400-km radius around Brussels.
Kredietbank member of the executive committee Remi Vermeiren said that foreign activities already contributed about a third of the bank's earnings.
He said that this came mainly from activities in south-east Asia, Ireland, New York and London.
Cockaerts said that the foreign expansion strategy was now focused on south-east Asia, where the bank hopes to open a fourth branch office in Manila, the Phillipines, in October.
"We hope to triple the number of branches in south-east Asia in the coming years," he said.
He added that the bank would also continue its expansion in eastern Europe, where it is active in Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
"We want to become the most active Belgian bank in eastern Europe," Cockaerts said.
The bank also said that adapting its computer networks to the switch into the new century will cost it nearly one billion francs ($32 million) -- as much as preparing for Europe's single currency.

"The cost of switching our systems to the year 2000 will be comparable to that of what the switch to the Euro will cost us -- just under one billion francs," executive committee member Herman Agneessens said.

Many companies have worried that the year 2000 will cause havoc in their computer systems, which were never programmed to cope with four digit dates. But few have so far put a figure on the cost of this so-called "Millennium Bug." ($1=31.15 Belgian Franc)
